title: Praying with imagination
hookLine: Ignatius puts you inside a gospel scene: the sounds, the dust, where you stand

lines: THE SAME POWER, TURNED TO PRAYER.
cards: Worry is a kind of imagination. So is replaying an old argument in the shower, word for word, in a room that's miles away. The mind is very good at putting a person somewhere they aren't.

Ignatius's Spiritual Exercises turn that same power toward prayer. Not to invent things about Jesus, but to step inside the scenes the Gospels already give, with their sounds and their dust, and find a place to stand.
Today the scene is a wedding, and the wine is about to run out.

teach.b: First, the place. Ignatius begins with what he calls composing the place: seeing the setting with the eyes of the imagination. How big is the room?
Is it hot? Where are the doors? Second, the senses.
Ignatius says to apply each sense in turn. What do you see? Who's there?
What do you hear, what do they say?
What do you smell and taste? What can you touch? You're not making up a new story.
You're filling in the one you've been given, the way you'd picture a story a grandparent told you.
Third, where you stand. Ignatius asks you to find yourself in the scene. A guest?
A servant? Near Jesus, or far away? Try it with John's Gospel: a wedding in Cana of Galilee.
Jesus is there with his disciples, and his mother, Mary.
The wine runs out. Mary says to Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "They have no wine." He answers, "Woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come."

teach.h: WHATSOEVER HE SHALL SAY TO YOU, DO YE.
teach.b: She turns to the servants anyway: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." He tells them to fill six big stone water jars to the brim, then draw some out and carry it to the steward. Fourth, what happens to you.
The steward tastes it, calls the groom, and says, "thou hast kept the good wine until now." John calls it the beginning of his miracles. The question is: where were you standing when that happened?
What did you feel? Catholics say God can speak through what surfaces there.

how: In Ignatian retreats Catholics pray through Gospel scenes one by one, imagining the setting with all the senses, and the wedding at Cana is the second Luminous Mystery of the rosary.

o: picturing a Gospel scene's setting with your senses
writing a new story about Jesus from scratch
choosing a quiet place in the house to pray

games.q: what's inside the practice — tap the pairs.
p: you have kept the good wine until now

s: praying with imagination means making up new stories about Jesus
it means stepping into the scenes the Gospels already give, and filling them in with your senses.
at Cana, Mary tells the servants to do whatever Jesus says
"Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye."
the steward says the worst wine was saved for last
"thou hast kept the good wine until now."

games.q: you're a servant at Cana. the wine is gone. a guest tells you to fill six huge stone jars with water, to the brim. what do you do?
o: fill them halfway and hope no one notices.
games.why: the servants fill them to the brim, draw some out, and carry it to the steward. it's wine, and the steward says the good wine was kept until now.

practice: Close your eyes and see the courtyard: lamps, music, children underfoot, the smell of roasting meat, then the whisper: the wine is gone.
Find where you are, a servant hauling heavy jars of water from the well, arms aching, or a guest, and watch Mary lean toward her son, watch the water poured out, and taste it.
Stay there; if you pray, you can speak to Jesus or to Mary there.

wordCard.voice: Compositio loci. Latin for composing the place, Ignatius's first step in imaginative prayer: seeing a Gospel scene with the eyes of your imagination. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the composition of place, Ignatius's first step in imaginative prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: step into the story. The story is already given; you find your place in it. Day two hundred thirty-nine, done.
